text.p: British motors and distribution group Inchcape Plc revealed static interim profits on Monday despite frenzied recent efforts to re-tune its corporate engine.
The internationally-spread group said that mixed markets for cars, consumer goods and financial services meant its recovery, following top management changes this year, was starting slowly.
The company reported pretax profits for the first six months a fraction lower than the same period last year at 82.8 million pounds ($128.6 million).
Chief executive Philip Cushing told reporters that the group's operating profit, excluding exceptional items, was broadly the same as last year for its on-going businesses.
"A number of things are happening and they are going in different directions," he said at a news conference.

In line with its new dividend policy, rebased at a lower level since drastic restructuring action started last year, Inchcape declared a basic interim dividend of 4.2 pence which it said compared with an adjusted year-ago payout of four pence.
The results were around market expectations, after the company warned in May that profits would be slightly lower.

Cushing noted that restructuring activity was still under way and some cost savings were yet to be realised from a slimming-down process that is meant to leave the group involved in fewer, stronger business areas.

The plan to work solely in distribution -- including motors, business equipment and the bottling of soft drinks -- is meant to include divesting two other areas; testing services and insurance broker Bain Hogg.

However, despite market expectation that deals for either or both of these transactions would be revealed on Monday, Inchcape said only that the plans to complete the divestments by the end of this year remained on track.
"All of these actions will enable us, over time, to achieve a simpler group with a simpler structure," Cushing said.

He added there had been "considerable interest" for the testing services area, with over 20 indicative offers for the unit which raised its operating profits 37 percent to 15.7 million pounds in the first half.
Cushing, who expects the sale to lead to a slight dilution in earnings per share, said a deal would be completed "in the very near future".
Inchcape also plans to demerge insurance broker Bain Hogg, which saw operating profit dip 20 percent in the first half due to softening insurance rates.

Overall, the company said it was expecting a good recovery in 1996, but noted that its forecast of an improvement on 1995's pretax profit of 146.8 million pounds was based on the performance of the entire group as currently constituted.
Cushing said he remained convinced that the slow haul approach, including an expensive plan to build up Coca-Cola bottling in Russia, would eventually pay off.
Analysts said there was little to either encourage or discourage any particular investment view on the shares as long as Inchcape had made no specific headway at the halfway stage.
By 1230 GMT the company's shares were down nine pence, or nearly three percent, at 293.5 pence in sluggish volume. ($1=.6439 Pound)
